div.head: II Cn 40
div.ab: Gyf man gehadodne oððe ælþeodigne þurh ænig þingc forræde æt feo oððe æt feore, þonne sceal him cingc beon for mæg ⁊ for mundboran, butan he elles oðerne (hlaford) hæbbe.
Gif man hadodne oððe ælðeodigne þurh anig þing forræde æt feo oððe æt fore, þonne sceal him cyninc beon for mæg ⁊ for mundboran, buton he elles oðerne habbe.
Si quis ordinatus uel alienigena seducatur in aliquo de pecunia uel uita, sit ei rex pro cognatione et aduocato, si penitus alium non habeat.
Gyf man gehadodne man oððe ælðeodigne man ðurh ænig ðingc forræde æt feo oððe æt feore, ðonne sceal him se kingc beon for mæg ⁊ for mundboran, buton he elles oðerne hæbbe.
Gyf man gehadodne oððe ælþeodigne þurh ænig þingc forræde æt feo oððe æt feore, þonne sceal him cingc beon for mæg and for mundboran butan he elles oðerne hlaford hæbbe.

Wenn jemand einen geweihten (Mann B) oder fremden (Mann B) durch irgend etwas schädigt an Geldwerth oder an Leben, dann soll diesem der König statt eines Verwandten und statt eines Beschützers sein — es sei denn, derselbe habe sonst einen anderen (Herrn G) —,
If anyone in any way wrongs a man in holy orders or a foreigner, in property or in life, then the king shall be to him in place of a kinsman and protector — unless he has another (lord, G) —,
If an attempt is made to deprive in any wise a man in orders or a stranger of either his goods or his life, the king shall act as his kinsman and protector, unless he has some other.
If a man in holy orders or a foreigner is for any reason defrauded of property or of life, the king shall then be for him in the place of a kinsman and protector, unless he has another.
If anyone conspires against the property or life of a cleric or a stranger in any way, then the king shall be his kinsman and protector if he does not have another guardian.

div.note: G's ‘(hlaford)’ is G's addition (missing from the other MSS, EGu and VIII Atr 33). Liebermann compares EGu 12.

From here to 48.3, the code draws mainly on VIII Ethelred and a related code of Wulfstan’s composition called erroneously “The treaty of Edward and Guthrum”; but it sometimes curtails, and sometimes expands from other sources, so I give it in full; 40, 40.1, 40.2, are from VIII Ethelred, 33, 34, 35, with omissions.
